{{Short description|American physicist (born 1938)}}
'''Eric George Adelberger''' (born June 26, 1938 in [[Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania]])<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref> is an American experimental nuclear physicist and gravitational metrologist.

==Biography==
He graduated from Washington-Lee High School (now known as [[Washington-Liberty High School]]), and then matriculated at [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech), where he was inspired by [[Richard Feynman]].<ref name=interview>{{cite web|title=Interview of Eric Adelberger by David Zierler on June 5, 2020|website=Niels Bohr Library & Archives, American Institute of Physics|date=24 September 2021 |url=http://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/44753}}</ref> At Caltech Adelberger graduated in 1960 with a B.S. and in 1967 with a Ph.D. under the supervision of Charles A. Barnes (1921–2015).<ref name=aip>{{cite web|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11408004.html|title=Eric G. Adelberger, Biography|website=American Institute of Physics}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis|author=Adelberger, Eric George|year=1967|title=A Study of T = 1, T = 3/2, and T = 2 States in Some Light Nuclei Using (He³,n) Reactions. Dissertation (Ph.D.)|website=CaltechTHESIS, A Caltech Library Service, California Institute of Technology|doi=10.7907/D6GW-RW22|url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/view/author/Adelberger-Eric-George.html|type=phd }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Eric G. Adelberger|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/tree.php?pid=115287}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Svitil, Kathy|title=Physicist Charles A. Barnes Dies|date=August 18, 2015|newspaper=Caltech News|url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/physicist-charles-barnes-dies-47561}}</ref> As a postdoc Adelberger was from 1967 to 1968 a research fellow at Caltech and from 1968 to 1969 a research associate at [[Stanford University]]. From 1969 to 1971 he was an assistant professor at [[Princeton University]]. At Seattle's [[University of Washington]], he was from 1971 to 1972 an assistant professor, from 1972 to 1975 an associate professor, and from 1975 to 2007 a full professor, retiring in 2007 as professor emeritus.<ref name=aip/> From 1978 to 1981 he was an associate editor for ''[[Physical Review Letters]]''.

His research deals with experimental nuclear physics (including fundamental symmetries in nuclei and nuclear structure) and experimental gravitational physics.

In the University of Washington's Eöt-wash Group,<ref>{{cite web|title=Eöt-wash Group|website=University of Washington|url=https://www.npl.washington.edu/eotwash/node/1}}</ref> he has investigated the validity of Newton's law of gravitation down to small distances, smaller than the previously tested minimum distances in the [[Millimetre|mm]] range. In 2007, the group was able to rule out [[extra dimensions]] larger than 44 [[micron]]s and hopes to be able to continue the experiment down to a few microns.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.021101|title=Tests of the Gravitational Inverse-Square Law below the Dark-Energy Length Scale |year=2007 |last1=Kapner |first1=D. J. |last2=Cook |first2=T. S. |last3=Adelberger |first3=E. G. |last4=Gundlach |first4=J. H. |last5=Heckel |first5=B. R. |last6=Hoyle |first6=C. D. |last7=Swanson |first7=H. E. |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=98 |issue=2 |article-number=021101 |pmid=17358595 |arxiv=hep-ph/0611184 |bibcode=2007PhRvL..98b1101K |s2cid=16379220 }} (over 1050 citations)</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/string-theorys-extra-dime|author=Minkel, J. R.|title=String theory´s Extra Dimensions must be less than half the width of a human hair|journal=Scientific American|date=January 16, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|author=Sokol, Joshua|title=Tiny Tests Seek the Universe's Big Mysteries|date=May 3, 2016|magazine=Quanta Magazine|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/tiny-tests-seek-the-universes-big-mysteries-20160503/}}</ref> With an improved torsion balance they also tested the [[equivalence principle]] for various substances and distances from 1 [[Metre|m]] to very large distances (from planet Earth to the centre of the [[Milky Way]]).<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.100.041101|title=Test of the Equivalence Principle Using a Rotating Torsion Balance |year=2008 |last1=Schlamminger |first1=S. |last2=Choi |first2=K.-Y. |last3=Wagner |first3=T. A. |last4=Gundlach |first4=J. H. |last5=Adelberger |first5=E. G. |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=100 |issue=4 |article-number=041101 |pmid=18352252 |arxiv=0712.0607 |bibcode=2008PhRvL.100d1101S |s2cid=18653407 }} (over 700 citations)</ref> They set new precision records in 2006 and 2008 for the [[Eötvös experiment#Table of measurements over time|Eötvös parameter]] with an accuracy that was not improved until the [[MICROSCOPE]] orbital satellite experiment in 2017.

In 1982 he received the [[Humboldt Senior Scientist Award]]. In 1985 he received the [[Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics]] for "his outstanding contributions in using nuclei to study fundamental symmetries, particularly studies of parity violation and isospin mixing."<ref>{{cite web|title=Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics Recipient, Eric G. Adelberger|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Adelberger&first_nm=Eric&year=1985}}</ref>  In 2021 he was awarded, jointly with [[Blayne Heckel]] and [[Jens H. Gundlach]], the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]] for "precision fundamental measurements that test our understanding of gravity, probe the nature of [[dark energy]], and establish limits on couplings to [[dark matter]]."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://breakthroughprize.org/News/60|title=Breakthrough Prize – Winners Of The 2021 Breakthrough Prizes In Life Sciences, Fundamental Physics And Mathematics Announced}}</ref>

Adelberger was elected in 1978 a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS),<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1978&unit_id=&institution=University+of+Washington}} (search on year=1978 and institution=University of Washington)</ref> in 1994 a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Eric G. Adelberger|website=Member Directory, National Academy of Sciences|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/eric-g-adelberger-ki1pla/}}</ref> and in 1998 a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Eric G. Adelberger|website=Member Directory, American Academy of Arts and Sciences|url=https://www.amacad.org/directory?search_api_fulltext=Adelberger&field_class_section=All&field_class_section_1=All&field_deceased=All&sort_bef_combine=search_api_relevance_DESC}}</ref>

In August 1961 in Arlington, Virginia, he married Audra Elizabeth Browman. They have two children.<ref name=interview/> Eric and Audra Adelberger have often backpacked and kayaked together and are long-time supporters of [[The Wilderness Society (United States)|The Wilderness Society]] and [[The Nature Conservancy]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Trailblazers: Audra and Eric Adelberger|website=[[Washington's National Park Fund|Washington National Park Fund]]|date=March 4, 2021|url=https://wnpf.org/2021/03/04/trailblazers-audra-and-eric-adelberger/}}</ref> In 1969, they made the first ascent of [[Mount Aleutka]] in Alaska.<ref name=AAJ>[https://publications.americanalpineclub.org/articles/12197211201/North-America-United-States-Alaska-Peaks-above-Glacier-Bay-Fairweather-Range ''North America, United-States, Alaska, Peaks above Glacier Bay, Fairweather Range''], Eric Adelberger, American Alpine Journal, 1972.</ref>
